opus-5.5.text:
I think the gap is mostly about everything that isn't the words themselves. If you look at transcription accuracy or the quality of synthesized speech, we're actually in a pretty good place now. The models understand what you say, and the voices sound quite natural. But when you actually try to have a conversation with one of these systems, it still feels like talking to a machine, and that comes from a lot of small things.

The first one is turn-taking. Humans are incredibly good at knowing when the other person is done speaking. We use intonation, pauses, context, and we often start formulating our answer before the other person has finished. Most voice systems still rely on fairly crude voice activity detection: wait for some silence, then respond. So either the model cuts you off when you pause to think, or it waits too long and there's this awkward gap. Getting latency down to a few hundred milliseconds while still not interrupting people is a hard problem.

The second is interruptions and backchanneling. In a real conversation you say "mm-hm" or "right" while the other person talks, or you interrupt to correct them, and they adapt in real time. Current models are mostly half-duplex: they listen, then they speak. Moving to models that can listen and speak at the same time, full-duplex, is, I think, one of the important steps.

Third, a lot of systems are still cascaded: speech-to-text, then a language model, then text-to-speech. Each step adds latency, and you lose information along the way. The tone of your voice, hesitation, emotion, emphasis all disappear once you turn it into text. So the model can't tell whether you're joking, frustrated, or unsure. More end-to-end audio-native models can keep that signal, but they're harder to train and it's harder to keep the reasoning quality of the text models.

And finally there's the data question. We have enormous amounts of text on the internet, but much less high-quality conversational audio, especially natural multi-speaker dialogue with overlaps and interruptions, and across many languages and accents. So I'd say the core intelligence is mostly there. What's missing is this layer of conversational dynamics, and I think that's what will make the difference between a voice interface you tolerate and one you actually prefer to typing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses turn-taking and pauses, but does not identify users slowing their speech to address voice models.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that users may retain a habit of speaking slowly after models no longer require it.

r003.rationale: It mentions limited conversational audio across languages and accents, but does not say voice models perform worse in French, Spanish, or German than in English.

r004.rationale: It attributes shortcomings to conversational dynamics, model architecture, latency, and data; it does not compare development effort with vision or coding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the gap is actually bigger than people assume when they first try these systems, and it comes from a few different places.

The first one is latency. When you and I talk, the time between you finishing a sentence and me starting to answer is something like two or three hundred milliseconds. Sometimes I even start before you're done. The classic pipeline for voice, where you do speech recognition, then feed the text to an LLM, then run text-to-speech, you're stacking three systems and the latencies add up. You end up at one, two seconds, and that completely breaks the feeling of a conversation. It feels like a walkie-talkie. So the first thing we wanted with Moshi was to collapse that into a single model that listens and speaks at the same time, in full duplex, so the model is always listening even while it's talking and can be interrupted, can backchannel, say "mm-hmm", things like that.

The second thing is that when you go through text, you lose almost everything that isn't the words. Emotion, hesitation, irony, whether someone is tired or excited, the rhythm of speech. The text transcript of a conversation is a very lossy compression of what actually happened. And on the generation side it's the same, the model should be able to decide how to say something, not just what to say. So you want the model to operate directly on audio tokens, or at least on something much closer to audio than text.

But then you run into the third problem, which is that if you work directly on audio, the sequences are very long and you have very little data compared to text. Text LLMs are trained on trillions of tokens of very dense information. Speech is maybe a few hundred thousand hours of data that's actually conversational, and the audio codec produces many tokens per second. So you need a good neural codec that compresses speech to a very low bitrate while keeping it intelligible, and you need some trick to still inherit the knowledge and reasoning of a text model. What we did was have the model produce an "inner monologue", a text stream aligned with the audio, so it keeps the intelligence from text pretraining while actually speaking in audio.

And honestly the last gap is just the quality of the dialogue data. Most speech datasets are audiobooks, podcasts, people reading. Real conversation with overlaps and interruptions is rare, and the models reflect that. So even when the architecture is right, the model can sound like it's reading to you rather than talking with you. I think we're close on latency now, we're getting there on expressivity, but the naturalness of real back-and-forth dialogue, that's still where most of the remaining work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses latency and dialogue naturalness, but does not identify users slowing their speech as evidence of unnatural interaction.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about people retaining a habit of slowing their speech after models improve.

r003.rationale: It does not compare voice model performance across English and other well-resourced languages.

r004.rationale: It attributes shortcomings to latency, audio representation, data, and dialogue quality, not to less development effort than vision or coding.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a fairly big gap between a model that can understand speech and generate speech, and one you can actually have a natural conversation with. If you have to finish your sentence, wait for the model to respond, and then wait for it to finish, it feels much more like exchanging voice messages than talking to someone.

In a real conversation, you interrupt each other. You start answering before the other person has completely finished. Sometimes a pause means you’re done, and sometimes it just means you’re thinking. The model needs to understand all of that, and it needs to keep listening while it’s speaking.

So I don’t think it’s only a question of making the voice sound more realistic. Latency and turn-taking are extremely important. You can have a very good answer and a very good voice, but if the timing is wrong, the interaction still feels unnatural.

r001.rationale: The response says natural conversation requires better timing and turn-taking, but does not identify users slowing their speech as evidence of unnatural interaction.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss people retaining a habit of slowing their speech after models improve.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between voice-model performance in English and other well-resourced languages.

r004.rationale: It attributes shortcomings to latency and turn-taking, without saying voice models have received less development effort than vision or coding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a gap between having a model that understands speech and generates speech, and having something you can really have a natural conversation with. When we talk, we interrupt each other, we pause, we change what we’re saying halfway through. The system has to understand whether you’re finished or just thinking, and it has to respond with very little latency.

If you have to wait a few seconds after every sentence, you start adapting to the machine. You make your questions more explicit, you wait for your turn. It becomes an interface rather than a conversation. So I think a lot of the challenge is getting that interaction right, in addition to improving the intelligence of the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response says people adapt by making questions more explicit and waiting for their turn, but does not mention slowing their speech.

r002.rationale: It does not say that people may retain a habit of slowing their speech after models improve.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between performance in English and other well-resourced languages.

r004.rationale: It attributes challenges to interaction and latency, but does not say voice models have received less development effort than vision or coding.
